title: -In- verb forms
summary: Passive verbs that put the spotlight on the thing acted upon: alisín, basáhin, kánin…
goals: Understand how -in- (passive) verbs differ from -um- and mag- (active) verbs
Build the infinitive, imperative, past, present and future of an -in- verb
Choose between the suffix -in and its alternant -hin
Recognise the irregular -in- verbs (bilhín, kánin, dalhín, nilutò…)
Build a passive sentence: verb + doer (possessive form) + object

blocks.t: The **-um-** and **mag-** verbs from Lesson 14 are **active**: they put the emphasis on the **doer** of the action, or on the action itself.

The **-in-** verbs are **passive**: they put the emphasis on the **object**, the thing that **receives** the action. That receiver then becomes the **subject** of the sentence. An -in- verb shows the action happening to the subject, and the doer does not even have to be named.

blocks.title: The main difference
items: With the active verb, the object is **not needed**: *Bumása ako* (I read) is a full sentence.
With the passive -in- verb, the object (**ang libró**) is **necessary** and cannot be left out.
In the passive sentence the emphasis is on the object (**ang libró**), not on the doer (**ko**).

blocks.title: Passive in English
blocks.t: English has passives too: *The book was read by me.* Tagalog uses them far more often than English does, so you will often translate an -in- sentence back into a normal active English sentence (*I read the book*).

blocks.title: -in and -hin
blocks.t: The ending **-hin** is simply another form (the book calls it an **alternant**) of **-in**. Section 3 shows when each one is used.

An -in- verb has five forms: the **infinitive** (to do), the **imperative** (a command), and three tenses: **past**, **present** and **future**. Where the -in- goes depends on how the root word begins and ends.
I. A root beginning with a vowel
**-in** is added either at the **end** or at the **front** of the root, depending on the tense.

blocks.t: II. A root beginning with a consonant and ending in a glottal catch
**-in-** is added either at the **end** or **after the first consonant**, depending on the tense. (The glottal catch is the fourth type of stress from Lesson 2, the one written with a circumflex ^.)

head: Form

Meaning
rows: doubled first syllable, with -in- between the first consonant and the next vowel

blocks.t: III. A root beginning with a consonant
**-in-** goes **after the first consonant**, but it becomes **-hin** when it is added at the **end** of the verb.

blocks.note: -in- slips in after the first consonant; the present and future double the first syllable.

blocks.title: A pattern you already know
items: **Infinitive and imperative** look the same: the root plus **-in** or **-hin**.
**Past**: -in- is put in (in front of a vowel, or after the first consonant). Nothing is doubled.
**Present**: like the past, but the first syllable is **doubled**.
**Future**: the first syllable is **doubled**, and **-in/-hin** goes on the end.

blocks.title: Spellings in the book
blocks.t: The book prints the future of bása as **babasahín** in this table, but as **Bábasahin** in its sample sentences.
**-in** is usually the suffix, and its alternant **-hin** takes its place in some cases. There are also irregular verbs that break these conventions.
Regular verbs

head: Rule
Root
-in- verb
rows: **-in** after a root that ends in a **consonant**
**-in** after a root that ends in a **vowel with a glottal catch**
**-hin** after a root that ends in a **vowel without a glottal catch**
blocks.title: Which suffix?

blocks.t: Irregular verbs

head: What happens
Root
-in- verb
rows: 1. The root is stressed on the **last syllable**: its final vowel is dropped before **-hin**.
2. The last syllable is a **VC or CVC** syllable (Lesson 2) with **i** or **o**: that i or o is dropped before **-in**.
3. The root begins with **l, w or y**: in the past and present the infix -in- becomes the prefix **ni-**.
blocks.title: Irregular -in- verbs

blocks.t: o changes to u
When the root's last syllable is **CVC with an o**, the **o changes to u** in the **infinitive, imperative and future**, and the verb then follows the regular pattern.

blocks.title: Notice
blocks.t: The present tense keeps the **o**: the sample sentences use **Ginágamot** (is being treated) from gamót.

blocks.title: Examples of -in- verbs

blocks.t: In a sentence with an -in- verb, the **doer** is always in the **possessive form** (Lesson 8): for example **ni Peter**, **ng batâ**, **ko**, **niyá**, **iyó**, **kanyà**, **ákin**, **átin** and **kanilà** (spelled here as the book prints them in this list; Lesson 8 writes kaniyá and kanilá).

The doer can also be **kitá**. The book describes it as a pronoun that is equivalent to **ikaw** (you) and **ko** (I) together; the book glosses it as *we*. See example 4 below, where it means *for you by me*.

blocks.title: Word order
blocks.t: The **verb** always comes **first**, followed immediately by the **doer**, then the **object**.

blocks.title: Action + doer + object
blocks.note: Was chosen / by the child / the book = The child chose the book.

items.en: Was chosen by the child the book. (The child chose the book.)
Was read by me the letter. (I read the letter.)
Will be eaten by Peter the fish. (Peter will eat the fish.)
Was bought for you by me the fruit. (I bought you a fruit.)

blocks.title: Reading the word-for-word line
blocks.t: The book gives each sentence word for word first (*Was chosen / by the child / the book*) and then in normal English (*The child chose the book*). Reading the word-for-word line helps you feel the Tagalog order.

blocks.title: Remember
items: -in- verbs are passive: the object becomes the subject (with ang) and the doer takes the possessive form.
Root with a vowel first: alisín, inalís, ináalis, áalisin.
Root with a consonant first: basáhin, binása, binábasa, babasahín.
-hin after a vowel without a glottal catch; -in after a consonant or a glottal catch.
Irregular: bilhín, dalhín, kánin, sundín, dakpín, and ni- before l, w, y (nilutò).

exercises.q: Which kind of verb puts the emphasis on the object (the receiver of the action)?
exercises.explain: -In- verbs are passive: the receiver becomes the subject.

exercises.q: In "Binása ko ang libró", who is the doer?
exercises.explain: The doer is in the possessive form: ko. The object ang libró is the subject.

exercises.q: Which sentence must have its object?
exercises.explain: With an -in- verb the object cannot be left out. Bumása ako on its own is fine.

exercises.q: What is the infinitive of alís (remove)?
exercises.explain: Root + suffix -in.

exercises.q: Which form of alís means "was/were removed"?
exercises.explain: Past: prefix in- + root.

exercises.q: Which form of bása means "is/are reading"?
exercises.explain: Present: -in- after the first consonant plus a doubled first syllable.

exercises.q: What is the past of basâ (wet)?
exercises.explain: Infix -in- after the first consonant.

exercises.q: Why is it basáhin and not basain?
options: bása ends in a vowel without a glottal catch
exercises.answer: bása ends in a vowel without a glottal catch
exercises.explain: -Hin is used after a vowel without a glottal catch.

exercises.q: Why is it sirain (to break) with -in?
options: sirâ ends in a vowel with a glottal catch
exercises.answer: sirâ ends in a vowel with a glottal catch
exercises.explain: -In follows a vowel with a glottal catch.

exercises.q: Which verb drops the final vowel of its root before -hin?
exercises.explain: Bilí is stressed on the last syllable, so its final vowel drops: bilhín.

exercises.q: Which verb drops the i of its root's last syllable before -in?
exercises.explain: Káin ends in a VC syllable with i, so the i is dropped: kánin.

options: Roots beginning with l, w or y

exercises.answer: Roots beginning with l, w or y
exercises.explain: lutò → nilutò, walís → niwalis, yarì → niyarì.

exercises.q: In which verb has the o of the root changed to u?
exercises.explain: In a CVC last syllable, o changes to u: inumín, future iinumín.

exercises.q: In an -in- sentence, what comes first?
exercises.explain: Verb, then doer, then object.

recap: -In- verbs are passive: the receiver of the action becomes the subject (ang), and the doer takes the possessive form (ko, ni Peter, ng batà).
Word order: verb + doer + object. Binása ko ang súlat. (I read the letter.)
Tenses: alisín / inalís / ináalis / áalisin and basáhin / binása / binábasa / babasahín.
-hin after a vowel without a glottal catch (basáhin); -in after a consonant or a glottal catch (alisín, sirain).
Irregular: bilhín, dalhín, kánin, sundín, dakpín; ni- before l, w, y (nilutò); o → u (gamutín, inumín).
